Text I

Firefighters are among the most respected professionals in any society. Their job goes far beyond putting out fires: they rescue people from car accidents, floods, and collapsed buildings, and they provide emergency medical care. Because their work is dangerous, firefighters must train constantly and stay physically fit. Every second counts when a life is at risk, so quick thinking and teamwork are essential.

Text II

Climate change has become one of the greatest challenges of our time. Rising temperatures are linked to more frequent and intense natural disasters, such as floods, droughts, and wildfires. Scientists warn that, without urgent action, these events will continue to grow worse. Reducing greenhouse gas emissions and protecting forests are seen as key steps to face this crisis.

Text III

The internet has transformed the way people communicate and access information. However, it has also made it easier to spread false news. A single misleading post can reach millions of users in minutes. Experts believe that the best defense against misinformation is education: when people learn to question what they read, they are less likely to be deceived.

Text IV

Knowing basic first aid can save lives. In the case of a cardiac arrest, for example, starting chest compressions immediately can double a victim's chances of survival. Yet many people are afraid to act because they fear making mistakes. Health experts argue that doing something is almost always better than doing nothing while waiting for an ambulance.

Text V

Water is essential to life, but it is not an unlimited resource. Although some countries have plenty of fresh water, millions of people around the world still lack access to clean drinking water. Pollution and waste make the problem worse. Protecting rivers and using water wisely are responsibilities that belong to everyone, not only to governments.

Text VI

When the river flooded the small town, hundreds of families lost their homes overnight. Volunteers from neighboring cities arrived quickly, bringing food, water, and blankets. Firefighters worked day and night to rescue those who were trapped. In the middle of the tragedy, the community discovered the strength of solidarity.

Text CB1B1

Firefighters are often seen as heroes, and for good reason. Every day, they face situations that most people would instinctively run away from. Yet their work involves far more than putting out flames. Modern fire services respond to car crashes, floods, chemical spills and medical emergencies, which means that a firefighter must be prepared for almost anything.

Training is therefore continuous and demanding. Recruits learn how to handle heavy equipment, how to move safely inside burning buildings and how to give first aid while waiting for an ambulance. Physical fitness matters, but so does the ability to stay calm when everything around seems out of control.

Perhaps the most surprising part of the job is how much of it is about prevention. Firefighters visit schools, inspect buildings and teach families how to reduce risks at home. In the long run, a fire that never starts saves more lives than the bravest rescue.

Based on the text above, judge the following items.

Text CB1B2

Wildfires have become more frequent and more intense across many parts of the world. Scientists warn that climate change is one of the main reasons: hotter temperatures and longer dry seasons turn forests into perfect fuel. Once a fire starts, strong winds can spread the flames over enormous distances in a matter of hours.

The consequences go beyond the destruction of trees. Smoke from large fires can travel thousands of kilometres, affecting the air quality of distant cities and putting vulnerable people at risk. Wild animals lose their habitats, and the soil, left without vegetation, becomes more likely to be washed away when the rains return.

Fighting these fires is extremely difficult and dangerous. For this reason, experts insist that prevention and early detection are essential. Satellites, drones and local communities all play a part in spotting fires before they grow out of control.

Based on the text above, judge the following items.

Text CB1B3

Knowing basic first aid can make the difference between life and death. In many emergencies, the first minutes are the most important, and help from a trained professional may still be several minutes away. A person who knows what to do can keep a victim stable until an ambulance arrives.

However, first aid is not only about dramatic situations such as heart attacks or serious accidents. It also includes simple skills, like how to treat a small burn, stop a nosebleed or help someone who is choking. These situations are far more common than most people imagine, and knowing how to react can prevent a minor problem from becoming a serious one.

Unfortunately, many people avoid learning first aid because they are afraid of doing something wrong. Experts argue that this fear is misplaced: doing nothing is usually far more dangerous than trying to help. Short courses, they say, are enough to give ordinary citizens the confidence they need.

Based on the text above, judge the following items.

Text CB1B4

Technology has transformed the way emergency services work. A few decades ago, someone who witnessed an accident had to find a public telephone to call for help. Today, a single call or message from a smartphone can send the exact location of an emergency to the nearest rescue team in seconds.

Modern control rooms use software that shows, on large screens, where every ambulance and fire engine is at any given moment. This allows operators to send the closest available unit, saving precious time. In some cities, drones are already being used to reach places that vehicles cannot access quickly, such as mountains or flooded areas.

Still, technology has its limits. Systems can fail, batteries can run out and networks can become overloaded during major disasters, exactly when they are needed most. For this reason, experts remind us that human training and simple, reliable methods should never be completely abandoned.

Based on the text above, judge the following items.

Text CB1B5

No firefighter works alone. Behind every successful rescue there is a team whose members trust each other completely. In a dangerous situation, a single mistake can put the whole group at risk, so communication must be clear and constant. Orders are given in short, simple sentences, and every member knows exactly what to do.

This sense of unity is not born overnight. It is built through years of shared training, long shifts and difficult experiences. Firefighters often describe their colleagues as a second family, people they can rely on when everything else fails. Such bonds explain why many of them find it hard to leave the profession, even after retirement.

Leadership also plays a crucial role. A good officer must make quick decisions under pressure, but must also listen to the team and protect its members. The best leaders, according to experienced firefighters, are those who never ask others to take a risk they would not take themselves.

Based on the text above, judge the following items.

Text CB1B6

Every summer, thousands of people head to beaches and rivers to escape the heat. Unfortunately, water also claims many lives each year, often because swimmers underestimate its dangers. A calm surface can hide strong currents, and a river that looks shallow may suddenly become deep.

One of the greatest dangers is the so-called rip current, a narrow stream of water that flows rapidly away from the shore. Swimmers caught in it often panic and try to swim straight back to the beach, exhausting themselves against a force they cannot beat. Lifeguards advise a different strategy: instead of fighting the current, one should swim parallel to the shore until it weakens.

Prevention, once again, is the best protection. Simple measures — swimming near lifeguards, respecting warning flags and never entering the water alone — can prevent most accidents. Knowing one's own limits, experts say, is just as important as knowing how to swim.

Based on the text above, judge the following items.

Text CB1B7

In many countries, part of the fire service depends on volunteers. These are ordinary men and women who, in addition to their regular jobs, dedicate their free time to helping others. When an alarm sounds, they may leave their homes in the middle of the night to fight a fire or rescue someone in danger.

Being a volunteer firefighter is not an easy choice. It demands the same training and courage required of professionals, but without a salary at the end of the month. What motivates these people, then? Most of them mention a simple desire to be useful and to protect the community where they live.

Volunteers also strengthen the bond between the fire service and the population. Because they come from the community itself, they understand its needs and are trusted by their neighbours. In small towns, where professional teams may be far away, a group of well-trained volunteers can be the only protection available for hours.

Still, volunteering has its challenges. Without enough support, equipment and recognition, many volunteers eventually give up. Experts argue that governments should invest in these groups, since a small amount of money can help save lives that would otherwise be lost.

Based on the text above, judge the following items.

Text CB1A2

Extreme weather events are no longer rare exceptions. Floods, landslides and heatwaves have become part of the routine of emergency services around the world, forcing firefighters to train for scenarios that, a few decades ago, seemed unlikely.

Experts insist, however, that response alone is not enough. Early-warning systems, urban planning and community education can prevent a heavy rain from turning into a tragedy. The cost of prevention, they argue, is far lower than the cost of reconstruction.

Based on the text above, judge the following items.

Text CB2A2

For a long time, emergency workers were expected to be tough and silent. Fear, grief and exhaustion were seen as personal weaknesses rather than predictable reactions to extreme situations. As a result, many suffered alone.

That view is slowly changing. Studies show that repeated exposure to traumatic scenes can lead to anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress. Experts argue that psychological support should not be treated as a luxury, but as an essential part of the job — because a team that is mentally exhausted cannot protect anyone properly.

Based on the text above, judge the following items.

Text CB3A2

Artificial intelligence is changing the way people work. Tasks that once required hours of human effort — writing reports, translating documents, analysing data — can now be performed in seconds. Unsurprisingly, many workers fear that their jobs may disappear.

Economists, however, offer a more nuanced view. According to recent studies, most occupations will not vanish; instead, they will be reshaped. The real challenge, they argue, is not the technology itself, but the speed of the transition — and whether workers will be given the training they need to keep up.

Based on the text above, judge the following items.

Text CB4A2

False information is not a new phenomenon, but the speed at which it now travels is. A rumour that once took weeks to spread across a town can reach millions of people in a matter of minutes. Social media algorithms, designed to reward engagement rather than accuracy, help the most emotional content circulate first.

Artificial intelligence has made things harder. Realistic fake videos and cloned voices are now easy to produce. Experts warn, however, that the greatest danger may not be believing what is false, but ceasing to believe in what is true.

Based on the text above, judge the following items.

Text CB5A2

Every year, more than a million people die on the world's roads. Most of these deaths are not random tragedies: speeding, drink-driving and the absence of seat belts or helmets account for a large share of them. In other words, they are predictable — and therefore preventable.

Countries that have managed to reduce road deaths did not rely on a single measure. They combined strict enforcement, safer vehicle design, better street planning and continuous education. Progress, experts stress, requires all of them working together.

Text (Praça exam, CBM/AL 2021 — summary of the original text, keeping the passages quoted in the items)

A first-of-its-kind analysis by more than 30 scientists concludes that the Amazon rainforest is most likely now a net contributor to global warming.

For years, researchers have expressed concern that rising temperatures, drought and deforestation are reducing the capacity of the world's largest rainforest to absorb carbon dioxide. Recent studies have even suggested that "some portions of the tropical landscape already may release more carbon than they store."

But "the inhaling and exhaling of CO2 is just one way this damp jungle, the most species-rich on Earth, influences the global climate." Natural and human activities in the region can warm the air directly or release other greenhouse gases.

"The damage, however, can still be reversed." Halting global emissions from coal, oil and natural gas would help, "but curbing Amazon deforestation is a must", along with reducing dam building and increasing efforts to replant trees. Continuing to clear land at current rates appears certain to make warming worse.

Based on the text above, judge the following items.

Text (Oficial exam, CBM/AL 2021 — summary of the original text, keeping the passages quoted in the items)

Forests are crucial to the functioning of the Earth: they provide homes for plants and animals, absorb rainfall, produce oxygen and absorb carbon dioxide, helping to keep global temperatures in check. "Ten thousand years ago, more than half of the world's habitable land was covered in trees"; since then, one third of those forests have been cut down to make way for agriculture and a growing human population.

Tree-planting programmes in rich countries have helped, but those countries continue to contribute, through their consumption, to the destruction of forests in poor countries. A study combining data on forest loss and international trade between 2001 and 2015 found that rich-country demand for goods led to deforestation mostly in tropical countries. "In G7 countries, for example, the area covered by forests increased every year between 2001 and 2015", but, after adjusting for trade, these countries contributed to a net loss of 20,000 square kilometers of forest elsewhere in 2015 alone.
